EN.about.techDirector.bio: Viacheslav Munister is an author, researcher, and digital heritage specialist. He is a member of the heritage associations En Quête de Patrimoine and Histoire d’en Parler. His work focuses on architecture, urban culture, collective memory, and the preservation and reinterpretation of cultural heritage through digital technologies.
EN.about.team.author-1785148692253-eva.bio: Eva Wyazenska is a culture journalist and screenwriter with a background in cultural journalism — art, photography, and how they shape the way we see the world. She's drawn to the people who make culture: how they think, where their ideas come from, and how they hold their sense of beauty. Interviews and essays are her way of letting culture speak through personal experience.

RU.about.techDirector.bio: Вячеслав Муністер — автор, исследователь и специалист по цифровому наследию. Он является членом ассоциаций наследия En Quête de Patrimoine и Histoire d’en Parler. Его работа сосредоточена на архитектуре, городской культуре, коллективной памяти, а также на сохранении и переосмыслении культурного наследия с помощью цифровых технологий.
RU.about.team.author-1785148692253-eva.bio: Eva Wyazenska — журналистка культуры и сценаристка с опытом в области культурной журналистики — искусство, фотография и их влияние на восприятие мира. Ее привлекают люди, создающие культуру: как они думают, откуда берутся их идеи и как они сохраняют чувство красоты. Интервью и эссе — её способ позволить культуре говорить через личный опыт.

UA.home.headline: Дитячий майданчик тихого дизайну
UA.home.intro: Досліджуючи простори та історії, що формують наш спосіб життя — з наміром, красою та відчуттям місця.
UA.about.techDirector.bio: В’ячеслав Муністер — автор, дослідник і спеціаліст з цифрової спадщини. Він є членом асоціацій спадщини En Quête de Patrimoine та Histoire d’en Parler. Його робота зосереджена на архітектурі, міській культурі, колективній пам’яті та збереженні й переосмисленні культурної спадщини за допомогою цифрових технологій.
UA.about.team.author-1785148692253-eva.bio: Eva Wyazenska — журналістка культури та сценаристка з досвідом у культурній журналістиці — мистецтво, фотографія та їхній вплив на спосіб, яким ми бачимо світ. Вона приваблена до людей, які створюють культуру: як вони думають, звідки беруться їхні ідеї та як вони зберігають своє відчуття краси. Інтерв’ю та есе — її спосіб дозволити культурі говорити через особистий досвід.

TR.about.techDirector.bio: Viacheslav Munister bir yazar, araştırmacı ve dijital miras uzmanıdır. En Quête de Patrimoine ve Histoire d’en Parler miras derneklerinin üyesidir. Çalışmaları mimarlık, kentsel kültür, kolektif hafıza ve dijital teknolojiler aracılığıyla kültürel mirasın korunması ve yeniden yorumlanmasına odaklanmaktadır.
TR.about.team.author-1785148692253-eva.bio: Eva Wyazenska kültür gazetecisi ve senarist olup, kültürel gazetecilik — sanat, fotoğraf ve bunların dünyayı görme biçimimizi nasıl şekillendirdiği alanında bir geçmişe sahiptir. Kültürü yaratan insanlara ilgi duyuyor: nasıl düşünüyorlar, fikirleri nereden geliyor ve güzellik duygularını nasıl koruyorlar. Röportajlar ve denemeler, kültürün kişisel deneyimlerle konuşmasına izin verme biçimidir.

DE.library.title: Titel
DE.hero.quote: "Epris journal ist nicht nur eine Veröffentlichung; es ist ein lebendiges Archiv der Dinge, die das Leben schmackhaft machen. Geboren aus dem Wunsch, langsamer zu werden und die flüchtige Schönheit unserer Existenz zu dokumentieren, dient dieses Journal als Zufluchtsort für Nachdenkliche, Neugierige und Ästhetische."
DE.about.quote1: "Epris journal ist nicht nur eine Veröffentlichung; es ist ein lebendiges Archiv der Dinge, die das Leben schmackhaft machen. Geboren aus dem Wunsch, langsamer zu werden und die flüchtige Schönheit unserer Existenz zu dokumentieren, dient dieses Journal als Zufluchtsort für Nachdenkliche, Neugierige und Ästhetische."
DE.about.bio: Mit einem Hintergrund in Kunstgeschichte und einer Leidenschaft für langsames Reisen gründete Mariia 2026 Epris Journal. Ihre Vision war es, einen digitalen Raum zu schaffen, der so greifbar und zeitlos ist wie ein gedrucktes Heft in einer alten Bibliothek.

DE.issue.letter.body: Eine Tür ist nie nur eine Tür — sie ist eine Membran zwischen Zuständen, zwischen der Wärme, die du verlassen hast, und der Kälte, in die du gleich eintreten wirst. Diese Ausgabe verfolgt, was Räume von uns halten, wenn wir von ihnen abwesend sind.

DE.about.techDirector.bio: Viacheslav Munister ist ein Autor, Forscher und Spezialist für digitales Erbe. Er ist Mitglied der Heritage-Verbände En Quête de Patrimoine und Histoire d’en Parler. Seine Arbeit konzentriert sich auf Architektur, urbane Kultur, kollektives Gedächtnis sowie die Bewahrung und Neuauslegung kulturellen Erbes durch digitale Technologien.
DE.about.team.author-1785148692253-eva.bio: Eva Wyazenska ist Kulturjournalistin und Drehbuchautorin mit Hintergrund in kultureller Berichterstattung — Kunst, Fotografie und wie sie unsere Sicht auf die Welt prägen. Sie fühlt sich zu den Menschen hingezogen, die Kultur schaffen: wie sie denken, woher ihre Ideen kommen und wie sie ihr Schönheitssinn bewahren. articles.title: Sandra Kantanen: Beyond the Lens of Traditional Photography
articles.author: EPRIS Journal
articles.excerpt: A focused opening paragraph for a new editorial story.

content.content: Finnish artist Sandra Kantanen approaches photography as a gateway to the imagined, rather than a tool for capturing objective reality. Her work reveals a unique, boundary-less technical philosophy, that pushes the medium beyond the constraints of the lens, challenging the viewer to question where the photograph ends and the painting begins.

At first glance, one might assume her ethereal landscapes are the result of mixed oil paints and traditional layering. In reality, these are photographs of natural environments-ranging from the forests of her native Finland to the mountains of Asia-subjected to profound digital and physical manipulation.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msma9wvbe77qf8.jpg
content.caption: Sandra Kantanen, Still life (Flowers 3), 2020

content.content: Born in Helsinki in 1974, Sandra Kantanen emerged as a key figure within the internationally celebrated Helsinki School of Photography. Her academic foundation was built at the Aalto University School of Arts, Design and Architecture in Helsinki, but the pivotal shift in her artistic trajectory occurred around the year 2000, when she moved to China as an exchange student.

Studying traditional Chinese landscape painting at the Central Academy of Fine Arts in Beijing, Kantanen became deeply influenced by Eastern philosophy. She was struck by how ancient masters did not aim to document the landscape, but to idealize and sublimate it.

During her travels through China's sacred mountains, she witnessed the stark tension between the pristine, spiritualized nature depicted in ancient silk scrolls and the harsh realities of modern industrial pollution and tourism. This dissonance became the catalyst for her practice: a lifelong pursuit to capture an "impossible" landscape – a space existing somewhere between memory, myth, and optical distortion.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msng6eycsbjvv4.jpg
content.caption: Sandra Kantanen, “Untitled (Mountain 7)”, 2010

content.content: While pixel-distorted landscapes are her most famous signature, Kantanen's broader photographic practice is remarkably diverse. She does not rely on a single technical trick; rather, she experiments across different series, constantly redefining how a photographic image can behave:

The Smoke Works and Pixel Manipulation: In her most renowned series, Kantanen physically intervenes in nature before the shutter even clicks. By releasing colored smoke bombs into remote forests – such as those near her home in Hango, Finland-she creates a surreal, psychedelic atmosphere that disrupts the mundane scenery. She then takes these digital files and subjects them to deep manipulation: blurring horizons, stretching data, and manually forcing pixels to flow so that the photograph mimics the fluidity of liquid paint.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msng9ejlxxhcjp.jpg
content.caption: Sandra Kantanen, “Untitled (Forest 21)”, 2021

content.content: Botanical Studies and Scanners: Shifting away from vast landscapes and pixel-stretching entirely, her floral still lifes and botanical works explore organic decay up close. For these, she often utilizes large-scale formats, long exposures, or even flatbed scanners instead of traditional camera lenses. These methods evoke the rich, allegorical depth of Dutch Golden Age painting, focusing on the intimate textures and slow passage of time in nature.
By moving fluidly between physical staging, scanner art, straight capture, and digital distortion, Kantanen constantly destabilizes our perception of what a photograph can be.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msngme9x0lctgn.jpg
content.caption: Sandra Kantanen, “Horizon”, 2005

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msngn7mg1xk589.jpg
content.caption: Sandra Kantanen, “Rain”, 2005

content.content: Over a career spanning more than two decades, Sandra Kantanen has earned widespread international acclaim for her innovative contributions to contemporary visual arts.
Her work has been showcased globally, with major exhibitions at venues like the Purdy Hicks Gallery in London, Paris Photo, and a comprehensive retrospective at the Turku Art Museum.

Kantanen's influence is cemented by her inclusion in the permanent collections of some of the world's most respected institutions, including the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, the Brooklyn Museum, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), and the Kiasma Museum of Contemporary Art in Helsinki. Her monographs, published by Hatje Cantz, serve as a testament to an artist who does not merely use technology, but bends it to the eternal service of beauty.

articles.title: Emily Kraus: Rhythm of the Moment
articles.author: Maria Ivanova
articles.excerpt: Inside the Canvas Cube, Emily Kraus Paints the Rhythm of the Present Moment

content.content: Emily Kraus's (New York, 1995) works left me unbothered by anything externally existing. I am frozen, trapped and stunned by the unidentified. It's almost like falling in love – you were not prepared, you didn't ask for it, yet it's one of the best feelings that can happen to the human being.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msjmgso0atp099.jpg
content.caption: Emily Kraus, Each in the other what each has to give, 2026. Photo by Ollie Hammick

content.content: When the art is a part of the artist's mind, body and soul – you can feel it from the innermost dedication to the practice. That form of connection can be compared to the billions of invisible thinnest threads that remain unbroken between the artist and the artwork, even when they are far apart. They are mutually nourishing and will never be independent again.
When you look at the painting and can almost physically feel the presence of the author - that's when the purest form of revelation is unfolding in front of you.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msjmzzvhzg92s2.webp
content.caption: Emily Kraus, Stochastic 20, 2023. Photo by Ollie Hammick

content.content: The first glance was not followed by the question "How?". I was too occupied dealing with jitters. The second one brought me back to consciousness, ready to be curious about how it was achieved.

Lack of immediate curiosity about technique corresponds to the artist's belief that the work should live on its own – the communication with the viewer relies on an individual reflection as the clearest translator of visuals.

Emily Kraus works in tandem with a self-invented structure, made of a scaffold with planks and rotating poles, on which the canvas is stretched. This approach gives a unique opportunity to rotate the surface and at the same time creates a cube-like enclosed space. From inside, the artist is applying the oil paints, and then rotates the canvas before the paint dries – as it moves through the poles, the paint gets smudged. The repeated steps result in the glitchy signature visual code.
As the canvas is geometrically structured, the result of the whole image is unknown until the end of the work, which takes approximately one month.

There is a beauty in the uncontrollable. The nature of each painting is not in the pursuit of visual appeal, but in a momentary decision, whether the following gesture belongs to this emerging artwork or not. Through this profound significance of the process, based purely on the artist's feelings, the painting accumulates a powerful, spiritual memory.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msjmraxbowmo4w.webp
content.caption: Emily Kraus, Fwooooop, 2024

content.content: This mechanism was influenced by the time when Kraus was studying in her second year at the Royal College of Art, which coincided with COVID-19 and the lockdown. She was assigned a cube studio 2.5 by 2.5 metres. The limited area of the room hampered Kraus's intention to paint with large gestures, experimenting with her body and space. To expand the possibilities of her practice in existing conditions, she stretched the canvas along all the walls using shower poles and wooden brackets. The canvas could be rotated, erasing the boundaries of the contained space.

The concept of confinement as part of a wider perception of space was on the artist's agenda before. Emily Kraus explored the boundaries of objects, places, and the relations between them. Moreover, she practiced meditation, which ultimately reconfigures the whole existing world, making it seamlessly broad and possible to totally fit in one's mind at the same time. Accumulating reflections along with a small studio space prompts a question about how one can find freedom when physically confined and how space cannot free us from the mind's cage.

As Lucian Freud stated – "Everything is a self-portrait". These words can't be more accurate when talking about art. The sublime essence of Emily Kraus's oeuvre is definitive, rather than chaotically formed – she holds a BA in Religious Studies from Kenyon College. The choice was influenced by Kraus's self-questioning of the meaning of life.

The profound influence of Emily Kraus on the contemporary art world is reinforced through the recognition by major institutions: as one of the Artsy Vanguard 2026, recipient of the Hopper Prize, and shortlisted for both the Hopper Prize and the John Moores Painting Prize, she continues to make discoveries through every new work, establishing her strong path.

articles.title: Against the Right Angle
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Five buildings that talked their way out of the grid – and the software, the metal, the money and the sheer nerve it took to build them.

content.content: Every architecture student is taught to revere the right angle, and every architecture student eventually notices that nothing outside the studio is at ninety degrees. Not the coastline, not the ribcage, not the river, not the way people cross a square – they cut the corner, always, which is why the grass on any campus dies diagonally before it dies anywhere else. The grid is not nature. The grid is a filing system. It won because it was cheap to draw with a T-square, cheap to price by the square metre, and cheap to defend in a planning meeting to a committee that had already stopped listening.

So for a century the curve was something you paid extra for and then justified in writing. Curved wall, custom formwork, a contractor breathing through his teeth, and a quantity surveyor wearing the expression of a man reading a hospital bill in a foreign currency. You were allowed exactly one – in the lobby, where visitors would see it and investors would feel it – and then the building went back to being a filing cabinet with windows, a nice reception desk and a coffee machine nobody had specified.

What ended the arrangement was not a manifesto. Manifestos had been available since 1919 and had built almost nothing. It was arithmetic. Between roughly 1990 and 2015, software borrowed from people who make aeroplanes and cars got good enough to describe a doubly curved surface precisely enough to cut it, cost it, insure it and – the unglamorous miracle at the bottom of this entire story – get a fabricator in a shed outside Zaragoza to produce panel 3,417 so that it meets panel 3,418 on a wet Tuesday in October, with a tolerance measured in millimetres and a foreman who does not care about your concept.

The five buildings below all sit inside that window, and they are habitually filed together under words designed to prevent thought: blob, parametric, organic, iconic – the last one deployed almost exclusively by people who want your signature on something. Look closer and they agree on nothing at all. One is a sculpture that happens to contain a museum. One is a landscape doing an impression of a building. One is a shopping centre having an existential crisis at 330,000 square metres. One is a traffic diagram that grew a skin and a Mercedes badge. One is a snowdrift with excellent acoustics and a free roof.

In every case the shape is the argument, not the wrapping paper. The interesting work – the part that survives the photograph – is establishing what each one is arguing for, who paid for the argument, and what it cost after the ribbon was cut. Because all five arrived with an invoice, and only some of them were worth settling.
01 · Frank GehryGuggenheim Museum Bilbao
Bilbao · opened 18 October 1997 · the sculpture that ate a city’s reputation

Reconstruct the pitch meeting for a moment. It is the early nineties. Bilbao is a port city with dying shipyards, a poisoned river, serious unemployment and a security situation that kept tourism reliably elsewhere. The Basque authorities propose that the remedy is a franchise of a New York museum, built on the derelict docks, designed by a Californian known internationally for chain-link fencing and an unresolved personal thing about fish. And they will pay for it themselves: eighty-nine million dollars.

The commission itself was decided in three weeks. Guggenheim director Thomas Krens shortlisted three architects – Gehry, Arata Isozaki, Coop Himmelblau – handed each ten thousand dollars, and asked for a concept. Isozaki sent sketches of an elliptical, four-storey block. Coop Himmelblau proposed transparent cubes. Gehry sent something that looked like nothing anyone had asked for, and got the job.

By every reasonable standard this should have ended in a public inquiry. Instead it became the most imitated urban gesture of the century, and the taxes it generated covered the construction bill inside three years.

• $89mconstruction cost
  • €100min taxes, first three years
  • 4 millionvisitors, first three years
  • 1.3 millionvisitors in 2025

Read those four figures in sequence, because they are the entire reason every mayor on earth has since wanted a strange building. Within three years the museum had generated an estimated €500 million of economic activity and about €100 million in taxes – the building paid for itself and then started sending money home. Almost no piece of public architecture in history can produce that receipt. It is why the phrase “the Bilbao effect” exists and why it has been misapplied roughly once a month ever since.

The design myth – Gehry crumples paper, hands it to an engineer, engineer weeps – gets the direction of travel exactly backwards. His office did work obsessively in physical models. The reason those models became a building rather than a lawsuit is CATIA, software written for the aerospace industry and adapted by his team to digitise the model and hand fabricators surfaces they could genuinely produce. Every panel is a numbered, tolerance-checked object with somewhere to be. The building looks like it was assembled during an argument. It is in fact among the most disciplined objects of its decade: a jazz solo that took nine months to write out in full.
It looks improvised. It is the most disciplined thing on the river.

Then there is the skin, which is the finest story in twentieth-century cladding and almost nobody tells it properly. Gehry originally intended stainless steel. What stands there is 33,000 titanium sheets, four-tenths of a millimetre thick, sixty tonnes in total – titanium being an aerospace metal nobody had ever used on a building at that scale, for the excellent reason that it costs a fortune.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-bilbao-titanium-detail.jpg
content.caption: Titanium, close up – sub-millimetre sheets, each curved individually, overlapping like fish scales. Photo: Jules Verne Times Two, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Except that in the early 1990s, briefly, it didn’t. The Soviet Union had built the Alfa-class attack submarine with a titanium hull; when Russia decommissioned the last of them, the metal flooded the world market and the price collapsed, undercutting stainless steel at precisely the moment Gehry was choosing a material. Which means the most photographed building of the late twentieth century is wrapped in decommissioned Cold War submarine stock. That shimmer over the Nervión is the peace dividend, rolled to 0.4 mm and bolted to a museum. No architectural historian would have dared invent it.

What Bilbao actually proved is more qualified than the export edition admits. The city also rebuilt its metro, cleaned the river, moved port functions downstream and ran a long, dull, properly funded regional plan into which the museum was inserted as the photogenic component. Cities that ordered the sculpture without the accompanying twenty years of work received a sculpture. Several received a very expensive empty sculpture – a lesson available free of charge and almost never taken.

My favourite thing about the building is the doorman. Guarding the entrance is Jeff Koons’s Puppy: a twelve-metre West Highland terrier upholstered in live flowering plants, watered and gardened continuously so that it never goes bald. A titanium cathedral of the international avant-garde, defended by an enormous dog made of petunias. Bilbao understood the thing its imitators never did – the whole enterprise works far better when it declines to take itself entirely seriously.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-bilbao-puppy.jpg
content.caption: Jeff Koons's Puppy on duty at the entrance – the avant-garde's least serious doorman. Photo: Jules Verne Times Two, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: 02 · Zaha Hadid ArchitectsHeydar Aliyev Center
Baku · opened 10 May 2012 · the floor that ran away up the wall

Zaha Hadid spent the first two decades of her fame as the most celebrated architect alive with almost nothing standing. She won Hong Kong’s Peak competition in 1983 with paintings that looked like shattered glass caught in flight; unbuilt. She won Cardiff Bay Opera House in the mid-nineties and watched the funding dissolve beneath a campaign that had a great deal to say about her being difficult and nothing intelligent to say about the design. For years she was the profession’s designated genius-in-waiting: brilliant, unbuildable, foreign, female – take your pick of which of those the committees were actually objecting to.
Baku is what happens when that imagination is finally handed a hillside and a quarter of a billion dollars.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-heydar-aliyev-night.jpg
content.caption: Heydar Aliyev Center, Zaha Hadid Architects, 2012. Locate the wall – there isn’t one. Photo: lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content:
• 57,500 m²floor area over eight levels
  • 74 mat the crest of the fold
  • 1,000seats in the auditorium
  • ~$250mestimated cost

The move is single and absolute: take the ground, lift it, fold it over the auditorium and the library, bring it back down. Plaza, façade and roof are one continuous surface and the building flatly refuses to say where any of them begins. Nothing performs visible heroics – the structure is a space frame concealed behind the white skin, sweating quietly, while the architecture out front maintains that none of this required effort. It is the swan principle, executed across 57,500 square metres.

Then you go inside, which is where the imitators are exposed. Curving the outside is now easy; the tell is whether the geometry survives the front door, or whether you are handed a rectangular room with a suspended ceiling and a fire escape sign. Here the auditorium is carved from identical logic – oak flowing from balcony to ceiling with no joint anywhere confessing that several different trades were involved. Hadid had been painting rooms like this since the 1980s, when they existed only as canvases in group shows. In Baku the painting and the building are the same object, which very few architects in history have got to say.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-baku-interior-stairs.jpg
content.caption: Inside the fold: stairs, balustrade and ceiling poured from the same continuous surface. Photo: Mahmoodrezamo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-heydar-aliyev-auditorium.jpg
content.caption: One thousand seats and not a right angle among them. Photo: Emin Allahverdi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Now the paragraph the coffee-table books leave out. The building is named for the late president of Azerbaijan and was commissioned under the government of his son, who succeeded him in office. It belongs to a very old genre – the national culture palace as portrait of the ruling family – and it went up in a city being remade at speed, with residents in the wider redevelopment area reporting demolitions and evictions they had not agreed to. When London’s Design Museum gave it Design of the Year in 2014, the prize arrived with a public argument attached, and the argument was not about the roof.

The swan-neck logic even extends to comfort. Tucked inside the folds are enclosed winter gardens several storeys tall, planted with real trees under glass, so the white curves have somewhere warm and green to land. It is an odd thing to grow indoors in a city built on oil rather than water – and it works precisely because nothing about the building apologises for the extravagance.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-baku-interior-garden.jpg
content.caption: One of the enclosed winter gardens – real trees, under glass, inside the curve. Photo: Mahmoodrezamo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Both things are true simultaneously, and the discomfort is the honest response rather than a failure of criticism. It is a masterpiece of surface geometry, probably the purest built expression of everything Hadid spent thirty years drawing. It is also a monument financed by an oil state to the father of its sitting president. A magazine that prints only the first sentence isn’t publishing criticism, it is publishing a brochure – and the building is strong enough to survive being described accurately, which is more than most monuments manage.
03 · Zaha Hadid ArchitectsGalaxy SOHO
Beijing · completed 2012 · four moons over the second ring road

Same office, same year, entirely different client: SOHO China, the developer run by Zhang Xin, which buys architecture the way other people buy watches – visibly, expensively, and with a clear understanding of what the signature does for resale. The brief was offices and retail on a major artery in central Beijing. The answer was four rounded volumes fused by bridges at several levels: 330,000 square metres across eighteen floors, with the space between them shaped into flowing courtyards instead of the customary windswept nothing developers leave between towers.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-galaxy-soho-bridge.jpg
content.caption: The bridges that fuse Galaxy SOHO's four volumes into one continuous route. Photo: Francesco Bini, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-galaxy-soho-courtyard.jpg
content.caption: Galaxy SOHO, 2012. The gap between buildings – normally where the bins live – promoted to principal room. Photo: HoweyYuan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content:
• 330,000 m²floor area – near six Heydar Aliyev Centers
  • 18floors
  • 67 mheight
  • 4fused volumes, bridged at several levels

The interiors are the genuine achievement and also the most quietly sinister thing in this essay. Balconies sweep past one another in unbroken bands; nothing squares off; the eye is never handed a corner where it can stop and rest. Stand on the third level and your gaze slides around the atrium like water going round a bath, and your feet follow, because that is what bodies do when the geometry keeps moving. It is genuinely beautiful. It is also, in retail terms, a machine engineered to stop you standing still long enough to decide you would rather go home.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-galaxy-soho-atrium.jpg
content.caption: Continuous bands rather than stacked floors: there is nowhere for your eye to sit down. Photo: Francesco Bini, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Which brings us to the fight, and it was a real one. In 2013, when the building was nominated for the RIBA’s Lubetkin Prize, the Beijing Cultural Heritage Protection Centre publicly objected, arguing that the development had “caused great damage to the preservation of the old Beijing streetscape, the original urban plan, the traditional hutong and courtyard houses, the landscape formation, and the style and colour scheme of Beijing’s unique vernacular architecture.” That is not a complaint about taste. It is a complaint about manners – a heritage body informing an international jury that the object under celebration had bulldozed the argument rather than won it.

And it lands, because a continuous, self-resolving geometry is superbly equipped to ignore whatever it happens to stand beside. A building made entirely of curves has no edges with which to meet anybody. It does not argue with the street; it declines to concede that the street was speaking. You can admire the object and still grant the point – I do both – and then notice the detail that settles it: everything generous about Galaxy SOHO faces inward. The courtyards are lovely, and they are private. That is an accurate description of a great deal of twenty-first-century development, and it is not a compliment.

None of which stopped Galaxy SOHO winning the RIBA International Award that same year – the letter and the trophy arrived within months of each other. International juries and municipal heritage bodies were, and still are, answering two entirely different questions.
04 · UNStudioMercedes-Benz Museum
Stuttgart · opened 19 May 2006 · the traffic diagram that grew a skin

Ben van Berkel and Caroline Bos do not begin with a shape. They begin with a problem in movement, draw the problem, and let the form be the consequence – which is why the practice is called UNStudio rather than something with two surnames on the door, and why this is the least self-indulgent building in this essay by a comfortable margin.

UNStudio won the competition for the site in 2001. The museum took five years to build – long enough that half of Stuttgart watched the trefoil rise out of a hole in the ground and had an opinion about it before a single car went on display.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-mercedes-blue-hour.jpg
content.caption: Mercedes-Benz Museum at blue hour – the twist reads even better lit from inside. Photo: Julian Herzog, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: The problem: Mercedes-Benz wants to tell two stories at once. The chronological one – here is 1886, here is the first automobile, keep walking through a century – and the thematic one, in which racing cars live with racing cars and delivery trucks with delivery trucks. Two narratives, one volume, and a visitor who will be justifiably furious if made to walk the first one twice to reach the second.

The answer is a double helix. Two ramps wind down through the building around a central void, never meeting, each carrying one of the stories, with crossings at every level. You ride to the top and descend. You may be a completist and take the century in order, or defect to the trucks whenever the mood strikes, and either way you are always going downhill and never lost. The plan is a cloverleaf of three overlapping circles with the middle removed – and the triangular atrium that produces is, quite deliberately, the shape of a Wankel rotary engine.
A shrine to the engine, in the shape of an engine, organised as a double helix. Corporate architecture is rarely this literate about itself.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-mercedes-benz-museum.jpg
content.caption: Mercedes-Benz Museum, UNStudio, 2006. It looks like that because of how you walk through it. Photo: Ank Kumar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content:
• 16,500 m²of exhibition space
  • 4,800 m²the footprint it stands on
  • 160+vehicles on display
  • 800,245visitors in 2023

Hold the first two numbers against each other, because they contain the whole trick: 16,500 square metres of exhibition standing on a footprint of 4,800. The building is nearly three and a half times larger than the ground it occupies, and it manages that not by stacking flat plates but by winding a continuous ramp through the air, so circulation and exhibition are the same square metre used twice. There is no wasted corridor anywhere in it. In a museum full of objects weighing as much as small buildings, it also means the twisting concrete has to span with almost nothing in the way of a bus.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-mercedes-benz-museum-facade.jpg
content.caption: Every band on the outside is a ramp on the inside, wearing a coat. Photo: Alexander Migl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: So this is, technically, the hardest object in the group and the only one whose difficulty is entirely invisible. The showmanship went into the structure and none of it into the photograph, which is presumably why it has never had the magazine career of Bilbao or Baku and – I suspect – exactly how the engineers wanted it. Eight hundred thousand people a year walk down it without once wondering how it stands up. That is not a failure of the architecture. That is the highest compliment the discipline has to give.
05 · MAD ArchitectsHarbin Opera House
Harbin · broke ground 2011, opened 2015 · a snowdrift you can buy tickets for

Ma Yansong worked in Hadid’s office before founding MAD, and the inheritance is legible in every surface. What he added is an argument about where the curves come from. MAD’s recurring claim is shanshui – mountain-water – that the Chinese building tradition is about landscape rather than object, and that architecture should behave like terrain instead of standing on it like a trophy. That is an easy thing to say in an interview and a hard thing to prove in aluminium. Harbin is the proof.

Consider the site. Harbin sits on the Songhua river in a province where winter is a six-month administrative fact, where the great annual festival is built from ice blocks sawn out of that same river, and where the temperature does things that make a Central European feel warmly towards his own miserable January. MAD gave it a low white mound in the wetland, clad entirely in white aluminium and read explicitly as a drift – a building at ease with snow because it is already shaped like snow. There are 470 parking spaces underneath it, because terrain is a metaphor and this is still China in 2015.

MAD won the project the ordinary way, for once: an open international competition in 2010, for a masterplan covering roughly 180 hectares of wetland along the Songhua – not just the theatre. The opera house is the one building from that plan the world actually looks at, but it was never meant to stand alone. It's the punctuation mark on a much longer sentence about the river.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-harbin-exterior-2.jpg
content.caption: Harbin Opera House by day: the aluminium reads as rock, ice or dune depending on the light. Photo: EditQ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-harbin-opera-house-panorama.jpg
content.caption: Harbin Opera House, MAD Architects, 2015. It settles into the wetland like weather that decided to stay. Photo: Jeremy Thompson, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content:
• 1,600+seats in the grand theatre
  • 400seats in the studio theatre
  • ~79,000 m²building area
  • 0tickets required for the roof

That last figure is the one that earns my respect, and it isn’t a joke. A public path is carved into the façade and climbs the outside of the building to a rooftop plaza anyone may walk up: no ticket, no performance, no dress code, nobody at the top checking whether you belong there. An opera house – the single most status-anxious building type in existence, a typology whose entire architectural history consists of staircases designed to be seen ascending – hands its best view to people who will never buy a seat. Every other opera house on earth spends its budget teaching you that the foyer is not for you. This one gives away the roof and asks for nothing.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-harbin-exterior-3.jpg
content.caption: The building's low, wind-carved profile against the Heilongjiang sky. Photo: EditQ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/epris-curves-harbin-opera-house.jpg
content.caption: The public ramp rises along the right-hand volume and carries straight over the top. Photo: EditQ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Then you step inside and the temperature of the architecture changes completely. The main hall is lined in Manchurian ash, milled into surfaces that read as eroded rather than assembled; MAD have described the guiding image as a block of wood hollowed out by hand. After all that arctic aluminium, walking into that warm grain does something almost physical – the pupils adjust, the shoulders drop. Ice outside, hearth inside. It is the oldest move in northern architecture, performed at the scale of a 1,600-seat theatre with a CNC mill.

That division of labour is the thing I keep returning to. Outside, curvature is climate. Inside, curvature is acoustics and warmth. Nowhere in the building is curvature merely curvature-because-it-photographs-well – and after two decades of buildings that were precisely that, the difference is not subtle. It is the difference between a form with a reason and a form with a publicist.
Afterwordwhat the curve costs

Twenty-five years on, the technology won and the rhetoric aged like milk. Nobody says “parametricism” aloud any more without a small apologetic cough. Doubly curved surfaces are ordinary industrial output; a competent mid-size practice can model, cost and procure one before lunch. The revolution succeeded so completely that it stopped being interesting, which is the customary fate of successful revolutions.

What has not become ordinary is keeping the results alive. A panelised skin is thousands of joints, and joints are where water goes to work. Sealant has a service life measured in years, not centuries, and 33,000 panels means 33,000 opportunities to be wrong. Masonry fails slowly and legibly – a stain, a crack, a conversation with a mason. A curved composite skin fails invisibly, then suddenly, then expensively. That invoice never appears next to the renderings, and it is the most reliable omission in architectural publishing.
Stone ages in public. Cladding just quietly stops being waterproof.

The second bill is urban, and much larger. A continuous surface is a closed argument: it resolves internally and leaves the street almost nothing to hold on to. Bilbao gets away with it by anchoring a waterfront that had nothing else and repaying its own construction cost in tax within three years. Harbin gets away with it by handing over the roof. Galaxy SOHO – on the evidence of the neighbourhood it landed in and the objection its own heritage body filed in public – does not. Curvature is not inherently generous or hostile. The only question that has ever mattered is whether the geometry left anywhere for the city to touch it.

So, a bet on which of these five reaches 2100 with its reputation intact. Stuttgart, because two stories genuinely needed to share one volume and a helix is the honest answer – the only building here whose shape could not be exchanged for a different one. Harbin, because a free public roof in a city that cold is a gift rather than a gesture. Bilbao survives on its receipts and its dog. The other two are magnificent, and magnificence, as any facilities manager will tell you, arrives with a maintenance schedule and a sealant contractor on speed dial.

None of which is an argument for returning to the filing cabinet. It is an argument for asking the question almost nobody asked between 1997 and 2015, in the euphoria of discovering that the software would let you draw anything at all: what is the curve for? Answer it honestly and you get Harbin, where the shape is the weather and the roof belongs to everybody. Fail to, and you get a spectacular photograph, a leak on the third floor, and a building that was better before it was finished.

  • Guggenheim Museum Bilbao – the museum on its own building: areas, galleries and the titanium skin – guggenheim-bilbao.eus
  • Association for Project Management – the project economics, and why titanium was briefly cheaper than steel – apm.org.uk
  • ArchDaily – Heydar Aliyev Center – drawings, structure and project data – archdaily.com
  • Dezeen – the open letter from Beijing’s heritage body over the Lubetkin nomination, 2013 – dezeen.com
  • UNStudio – Mercedes-Benz Museum – the trefoil plan and double-helix circulation, from the architects – unstudio.com
  • MAD Architects – Harbin Opera House – building area, seating and the public rooftop route – i-mad.com

articles.title: Polish Design: Woven From Memory
articles.author: Maria Ivanova
articles.excerpt: How does the sensetivity of Polish designers towards cultural heritage shape the design scene

content.content: Contemporary Polish design has arrived at a moment of profound, quiet maturity. To walk through the studios of today’s leading architects and furniture designers is to encounter a language of rigorous minimalism, tactile raw materials, and a deliberate structural honesty. Yet, this modern clarity is not a rejection of the past - it is the culmination of a century-long dialogue regarding what it means to create with a national soul.

To understand this current precision, one must look back to the Young Poland (Młoda Polska) movement of the 1890s. Emerging at a time when Poland was politically erased from the map, the movement acted as a vital act of cultural resistance. Polish artists, much like their peers in the British Arts and Crafts movement, rejected the soulless standardization of the Industrial Age. Instead, they sought to construct a national identity through the arts, fusing architecture, furniture, and textiles into a "total work of art" that was heavily steeped in local folklore, symbolism, and a romanticized connection to the land. It was a movement born from a desperate need to preserve a culture that was under existential threat.

Modern Polish design has inherited this deep-seated ethos of artisan integrity, but it has undergone a striking evolution in its execution. Where the artists of Young Poland once relied on intricate, heavy ornamentation to assert their heritage, today’s designers have chosen the path of subtraction. They have systematically stripped away the romantic veneer of the past to reveal the structural skeleton underneath.

The result is a design language that feels unmistakably Polish, not through the repetition of folklore, but through an unwavering commitment to architectural discipline. In these contemporary spaces, the warmth of tradition is now expressed through the inherent quality of materials – the grain of wood, the weight of stone, and the thoughtful geometry of a form. It is a transition from the decorative to the essential.

By focusing on the quiet beauty of proportion and the tactile reality of the everyday, today’s creators have moved beyond the struggle to define an identity. They have built one that is self-assured and globally resonant – a sophisticated bridge between the ancestral pride of the 1890s and the minimalist, structural reality of the present.
Wiktoria and Filip Bielicki

Wiktoria and Filip Bielicki operate at the intersection of structural rigor and tactile sensitivity, creating objects that function less as mere furniture and more as deliberate anchors within a space.

The first sight on their cabinets give us a riddle. The convex surface of the doors hide more than an abstract forms - light and shadow interplay framed the cast of branches, leaves, snags, trunks and mosses that are laid in chaotic composition. Later the intersection of natural objects are scanned in 3d for further incremental aluminum sheet forming by KUKA robot.
Technologies become an instrument of detailed stamping of fragile organic structures with elaborate surfaces, that freeze in time forever.

The visual stealthiness and modesty of represented natural elements is achieved by the use of matte mono material and simple geometrical forms of cabinets. The part of the design is allocated to light - more accurately, to the shadows caused by it - convex relief is a consistent dialogue with the environment.

The idea of preserving the nature without a direct use of materials sourced from it is an example of impressive contemporary Polish design, that prove its ingenuity deprived of radical independence from the past and the environment.
Zofia Wyganowska

Projects under the signage of Zofia Wyganowska Studio are executed with a rigorous attention to Polish heritage, bridging the gap between historical craft and contemporary restraint. The interiors are characterized by a light, airy quality, where tactile materials and contrasting volumes exist in a state of deliberate equilibrium. Operating within a strictly curated color palette, Wyganowska emphasizes clarity, allowing self-explanatory furniture - often crafted from raw, natural materials - to dictate the mood of the space.

A vital component of her signature aesthetic is the handling of surface texture. Whether achieved through intentional craftsmanship or the patient patina of time, these surfaces grant her projects a depth that feels both lived-in and meticulously composed. This commitment to materiality is matched by her active integration of contemporary Polish art and design, effectively turning her interiors into galleries of local creative dialogue.

This synthesis of tradition and modernism is perhaps most evident in her collaboration with the niche perfume store, Mood Scent Bar. Within this retail environment, Wyganowska integrates pajaki as a rhythmic counterpoint to the store’s minimalist architecture. By suspending these intricate, geometric structures against the sleek, stark lines of the display shelves, she recontextualizes folk art into a striking sculptural installation.

content.caption: Mood Scent Bar

content.content: Karolina Merska

Mentionig "pajaki" is inseparable with art historian Karolina Merska, who gives a renaissance to this traditional Polish element. Pajaki (from pl. spider) is a traditional pendant accessories made out of straw and paper, which were hanging from the ceiling in the village houses. It’s believed that they bring luck, protect from evil and deliver prosperity.

As in its historical roots, pajaki continuous to bring joy in the modern interiors. Hand-crafted suspended structures with various details is embraced in dynamism. The movement of decorative accumulations with pompons, straw and flowers is a focus of attention, reminding about rich and eclectic heritage of Poland.

Yet, beyond this vibrant exterior lies a profound architectural discipline. Merska does not merely replicate the past; she refines it, distilling the complex, cosmic geometry of the pajaki into a form that resonates with contemporary silence and light. By isolating these intricate silhouettes, she forces a reconciliation between the ephemeral nature of the materials – straw and paper – and the enduring weight of cultural memory.
Ala Savashevich

Ala Savashevich’s handwoven works operate as a stark, intellectual subversion of the tactile warmth we typically associate with loom-based traditions. While her choice of technique is deeply embedded in the lineage of Polish folk weaving, she systematically strips away the decorative joy of the craft to expose its underlying structural logic.

In these pieces, the act of weaving is no longer a search for aesthetic softness or domestic ornamentation. Instead, it becomes a method of mapping tension. By utilizing raw, sometimes industrial materials or monochromatic palettes, she transforms the fluid movement of the hand into a static, architectural grid.

It is here that the dialogue with Polish tradition becomes most visceral. Traditionally, the weaver’s labor was a communal, stabilizing force, a way of binding the domestic environment together. Savashevich retains this binding quality, yet she directs it toward a critical examination of social and historical boundaries.

Her textiles function like blueprints of restraint – they are woven with the same obsessive precision as her sculptural objects, forcing the viewer to confront the fact that our traditions are not merely decorative overlays, but are, in fact, the very warp and weft of our ideological fabric. It is a brilliant, quiet form of resistance, where the ancient craft of the loom is turned into a lens for modern, analytical inquiry.
Ania Jaworska

Ania Jaworska is an architect and designer whose practice operates at the precise intersection of fine art and architectural theory. Having honed her craft through formal education at both the Cracow University of Technology and the Cranbrook Academy of Art, she approaches design not as mere product creation, but as a conceptual interrogation of space and behavior.

Her work is defined by a bold, reductive vocabulary – frequently utilizing geometric rigor to challenge our perceptions of utility. The SET series, showcased at the Volume Gallery, serves as a poignant example of this methodology. In pieces like the Unit 2B (Coffee Table), Jaworska moves beyond the surface-level function of furniture, instead treating the object as an archetype. By employing stark, monochromatic palettes and monolithic forms, she strips away the superfluous to reveal the essential masses.

Her design language is an intellectual exercise in balancing playfulness with profound structural discipline. Jaworska’s practice is a testament to the fact that when form is executed with absolute clarity, it ceases to be just an object and becomes a deliberate, spatial statement.
Marcin Rusak

Marcin Rusak’s creative practice is deeply rooted in his personal heritage as the descendant of several generations of flower growers, a background that anchors his exploration of ephemerality, nature, and the concept of beauty. This connection to Polish agricultural traditions serves as a vital bridge between the historical significance of the land and a contemporary design language that questions our modern habits of overproduction and excess consumption.

His studio acts as a laboratory for the intersection of preservation and decay, creating works that challenge the perceived permanence of our material world. By treating his projects as evolving experiments, Rusak reframes the mundane details of daily life into profound experiences, using botany as a lens to reconsider our relationship with time and aesthetic value.
This approach aligns with the broader trajectory of modern Polish design, which seeks to transcend mere decoration by imbuing functional objects with narrative depth.

Nowadays Polish Design is a quintessence of devotion to the craftsmanship, that has proclaimed the cultural identity for decades. Aspiring to create against the backdrop of utilitarian minimalism, architects and designers translate their vision, continuing to shape a unique national narrative that amazes the creatives around  the world.

articles.title: Tadao Ando
articles.author: Maria Ivanova
articles.excerpt: Architecture beneath the tangible

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrt3zzweaxc7gh.jpg

Tadao Ando is one of the most influential architects of 21st century, 
who challenges the conventional definition and boarders of architecture. 
His unique approach showcased the rethinking of traditional Japanese 
principles through bold shapes, materials and spatial organizations. In this article we are going to reveal the core principles of his philosophy and its cues.
Background and Influences

Tadao Ando was born in Osaka (once called the “City of Water”) in 1941. He was born as the first 
twin, but then his parents decided to separate them. Tadao Ando was raised by his maternal 
grandmother in a simple neighborhood with a variety of craftsmen, woodworkers, and others. He spent days in 
their workshops  working with materials, builds airplanes and ships. It would be fair 
to say that this environment served as a foundation for the life-learning the renowned architect 
pursued.

From the age of 17, being influenced by his twin, Ando started to take up boxing. This sport has 
shaped his fighting spirit, which helps him in the future life.

In the early 20s, during the period of 1962-1969, after the Japanese ban was lifted, Tadao Ando took a 
trip to Europe, United States and Africa. He took a ship from Japan to the Soviet Union, where he 
went to Moscow with a week-long Trans-Siberian Railway. During that trip, he saw many countries 
and had an indisputable architectural experience, which would later become the basis of his famous 
quote:
“Architecture encompasses things that cannot be captured through the media. This is why architects must travel; architects are made through traveling”

Despite an acquaintance with numerous buildings in different countries, his desired destination for 
this journey was the heritage of Le Corbusier, who nourished his interest in architecture.

He got to know a French iconic architect by chance, finding his manuscript in an old secondhand bookshop. The value of this book lies not in the actual price but entirely in the footprint it left on Tadao Ando's life and career. The architect was fascinated by the projects and recalled that he had traced Corbusier’s early sketches so many times that the paper had become almost black. Furthermore, he admitted that while thinking about his own projects, he thinks about what Le Corbusier would have said about it and how he would evaluate it.

Tadao Ando didn’t receive formal training in any field, but opened his firm, “Tadao Ando 
Architect &amp; Associates,” in 1969 in Osaka, after returning from his long “field-study” in various 
countries, that, along with the Japanese spatial philosophy and books about architecture, shaped 
his way of thinking. Ando didn’t pursue an empirical way of learning by being a student of other 
architects, as his stubbornness and temper always led to dismissal.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrt41vsy86q9zs.jpg

The first attempts in design were with small wooden houses, interiors, and furniture. However, it's 
been 6 years of his practice before he completed the Row House (Azuma House), which gave him praise 
and recognition through the prize from the Japanese Architectural Association.

content.caption: Row House, 1976

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrt4d5ef1m1idz.jpg
content.caption: Rokko Housing, 1981-1998

content.content: Another project executed in the late 1970s, the Rokko Housing complex, was widely published and emphasized its importance in the architectural field beyond the local context. It's inserted into a slope at the foot of the Rokko Mountains, allowing panoramic views. Remaining loyal to the rigid grid and geometry, Tadao Ando nonetheless worked in a more elaborate form and composition, proving that simplicity is a conscious, but not limiting, choice for his philosophical embodiment.

The following projects strengthened the tendency for transboundary recognition. Such buildings 
as Church on the Water (1988) in Tomamu, Hokkaido or Church of the Light (1988-89) in Ibaraki, 
Osaka promote their author as an architect with 
a deep spiritual understanding of the space and nature connection. In spite of Japan being the only 
country to host his projects by the end of 1980, the influence has changed the status quo, and in 
1991 the Modern Museum of Modern Art gave an exhibition dedicated to Tadao Ando, indirectly 
labeling him “one of the preeminent living architects in the world”.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrt4lpc2fr80ye.jpg
content.caption: Church on the Water (1988)

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrt5ophk1v5q4j.webp
content.caption: Church of the Light (1988-89)

content.content:
Throughout the whole career till nowadays Tadao Ando designer more than 300 constructed 
projects all over the world.
We can name three main pillars of his approach, influenced by the background:

Traditional Japanese architecture. Growing up in Japan in residential common dwellings inevitably influences the perception and the initial idea about certain aspects. However, according to Tadao Ando's words in the interview with Toshio Okumana, he doesn’t use any traditional architectural elements, but wants to evoke the feeling of it, through adaptation of emotional sensitivity, rather then direct physical elements. The last is an artificial addition to the building, which nevertheless keeps it standardized without enhancing the perceptive depth and significance, which are laid between the obvious presence of elements. The approach is not mimicry of the form, but the mimicry of feeling.

Ephemeral and intangible over physical. Tadao Ando is inclined to give a predominant role to the ephemeral elements in architecture, which is commonly recognized as solid and structural matter. However, the consistent presence and monumentality perform as a background for important factors, such as light, which deal with subtle susceptibility. Most probably this intention is directed by the experience which architect exposed himself to at teenage years: around the age 15, he went to study old rural houses to impress upon himself the traditional Japanese space.

Study of architecture through travelling and experience of the space. As it was a major part of his self-taught architectural education, the concentration on the feeling and emotions in his own projects keep the same significance.
Architectural Philosophy and Design Principles
“Tension in acceptance”

There is a strong belief penetrating the Japanese architecture framework, concerning the blend of 
the outside environment and the interior space. The borders between the above-mentioned dual 
definitions are meant to be softened, visually and physically melting into each other to avoid the 
rigid division. This idea of harmonious coexistence of antagonist spaces found its base in 
philosophy and historical relationship with nature, and it is supported by many strategies in the 
Nippon Koku.

However, Tadao Ando had directly defined, both verbally and in his projects, that his mindset is occupied with the idea of the necessity of rejection. According to his words, acceptance means setting down one’s guards, allowing for excessive inflow into the interior, which by these means is losing its certainty. The reason lies in the absence of tension in the act of rejection. Thus, the renowned architect is convinced that tension should be an indisputable part of acceptance as well as in the architectural context, tension signifies the confrontation between exterior and interior, underscoring the importance of the places in a building of their contest.

Walls, as the strongest border between the intrinsic and extrinsic, play a significant role in Tadao 
Ando's approach �� he works with thin materiality and by specific positions with intervals creates 
openings to allow the structure accept even in the act of prime rejection. Walls are perceived as a 
“sword”, which cuts the landscape, sky, wind, and sunlight in order to promote new disclosure. 
This act of manifestation is not seen as a cruelty to the exterior, but as a ceremonial and sacred 
deed, with assimilating nature as an equal part of architecture.
“Essentials of human life”

Tadao Ando is known for his minimalist approach, reflected by the boldness and fine clarity of his 
ideas. It touches upon walls and the spatial arrangement. However, the simplicity of the walls and 
their raw forms and finishes is not based on mere aesthetic considerations; its foundation is deeply 
rooted in Ando’s philosophy of life. He believes that contemporary culture is characterized by a 
loop of satisfying unconstrained and never-ending desires, so he raised a silent question about what 
contributes to the richness of life and what is essential. Through his projects, he is 
conveying a supposed answer with the underlying meaning of true abundance, which is translated 
in 
simplification, elimination of surface decoration, and employment of symmetrical 
compositions.
Architectural silence

The striking quietude of the architect’s projects is defined by his faith that architecture should 
remain silent and let the presence of changing nature to be dominant, staying tolerant to the passage 
of time, hourly, daily, and seasonal transformations, that nurture a finer sensitivity in humans.
Revitalization of nature connection

According to Tadao Ando, the population growth and urbanization after World War II made it 
impossible to preserve the core base of traditional Japanese residential architecture – connection 
with nature and openness to it. In his projects, this principle goes beyond the mere tribute to the 
historical value, but rather is performed as a main builder of the concept, shape and mass 
distribution.
“Voids as a part of architecture”

If the architecture can be compared to sculpture, than its fair to make a correlation with the void
mass relation. Even if the observation of these two media is irrelevant, it helps to scale down the 
building structure and start to perceive it mainly in masses. Tadao Ando had a strong persuasion 
that it's essential to leave blank spaces in project design, and endow them with the same 
significance as the man-made intervention. The interstices should bear their intrinsic logic within 
the structure, and this approach enhances the value and the individuality of the architecture.
Light is an important controlling spatial factor

Tadao Ando has a focal focus on the role of light in the built environment. He believes that the architecture is not about walls, floor, and ceiling, but about the contained world outside. This space can be changed not only by the form, but also by the means of directed light. If the more grounded correlation is to be made, the way light defines the character of the rooms resembles the fireplace in a traditional home. The light can be manipulated in different ways to create a gentle environment for habitats.
Restricted vocabulary

This principle of Tadao Ando’s works is directly perceived by every observer, even the one with 
no experience in architecture or any related field. The paradox of the limited use in different 
categories of built structure is the correlation between the level of limitations and the visual and 
sensory effect. Moderate material palette, strictness of forms, and dignified simplicity of spatial 
relations result in a visually attention-getting object, also through the difference with the natural 
and man-made environment.

One of the most remarkable examples, that, according to the architect's words, encapsulates all 
of his principles and emphasizes the essence of the whole oeuvre is a Row House Sumiyoshi 
(Azuma House) in Osaka, Japan, constructed in 1976. The residential module is 
located in a dense urban environment, and its rectangular shape is divided into three equal parts, 
where the middle is dedicated to the open courtyard, connecting habitats with nature, exposing 
them to changing weather conditions every time they want to go from one part of the house to the 
other and emphasizing the priority of nature even in the challenging conditions. The equality of 
the open part and its obligatory binding function encapsulates Tadao Ando's approach to 
incorporate blankness.

The chosen material is unfinished concrete, which is also a substantial characteristic of the prominent architect. It creates a moderate appearance of the house, not trying to evoke warmer feelings, but rather keeping true to the material and shifting the attention to the intrinsic values and meanings. The envelope of the Azuma House is not designed to impress; the facades of Tadao Ando’s buildings do not respond to the modern expectations of superficial satisfaction in every aspect.

Tadao Ando's philosophy is unique, and it can't be more accurately conveyed than through his 
words. In his essay “A Wedge in Circumstances,” he explained his approach to the residential 
space – the house is a stage for living; therefore, the manner of entertaining and the paths are very 
important. He is convinced that the architectural plan shouldn’t be perceived from the inside – 
once a visitor steps into the space, it's not important for him/her to comprehend the layout, he/she 
should cognitively comprehend the embraced space. That’s the reason for asymmetrical, variable, 
and unpredictable space relations in his projects.

articles.title: Art that makes you smile
articles.author: Maria Ivanova
articles.excerpt: I believe that when you introduce playful objects into an environment, it expands the boundaries of the mind. It gives you non-verbal permission to think freely - not just to push against conventional frames, but to forget they even exist.

content.content: There is a preconception that pleasure derived from an art piece, or the smile it evokes, somehow lowers its value and strips it of the grand title of “Art.” However, this is simply not true.

Art can speak loudly without words, making it an indisputable instrument for materializing self-reflection or addressing social and political concerns. Yet, if we look at the etymology of the word, “art” is not historically related to “seriousness” or anything of the sort; it takes its roots in hand-related craft, brilliantly mastered and executed. This origin automatically deprives art of any mandatory obligations and legitimizes its right to just be.

As was mentioned, art serves as a reflection of social, political, gender, or other issues. It can be a medium for personal introspection or a vehicle to deliver complex ideas in diverse shapes and forms. But an artist still can create playful objects following an intrinsic desire to feel the material, to experiment with shapes and colors, to master techniques, and to bring a piece of joy to everyday life. And being playful is not synonymous with being superficial. All objects carry the background, beliefs, vision, intentions, and concerns of their creators - they are simply expressed through a different lens.

Taking everything too seriously is a dead end - and it certainly shouldn't cross your mind when you are choosing a new piece for your home. Ultimately, the baseline is your personal preference. If you only approve of strict beige and black forms, or conventional mediums and subjects, that is wonderful! My only concern is when people don't even allow themselves to consider a piece that might spark a moment of delight. We constantly hear: “It looks so great, it will go beautifully with my walls and my other paintings.” But next time, try asking yourself a different question: Does it make me smile? Colorful and playful objects possess a unique quality that others lack - they inject pure happiness into a room. We don’t think about this often enough, focusing instead on how trendy a piece is or how it makes our home look. But how does it make us feel?
Colorful and playful objects possess a unique quality that others lack - they inject pure happiness into a room.

Interior design is not just a setting, a static picture, a composition, or a color palette. It is a living environment that embraces and enswathes you. We are used to considering an interior as an external component of our existence, positioning ourselves merely as spectators. In reality, the moment we step into a space, we are absorbed by it, invisibly adopting its mood and yielding to the irresistible influence of its atmosphere. There is even a specific branch of science - neuroarchitecture - that studies how the environment affects our cognitive performance, as well as our psychological and physical well-being. Mostly, these effects are triggered by spatial characteristics, color psychology, and the tactile properties of materials. However, there is one element that often falls off this scientific list but still has a major impact on how we experience a space: details filled with irony and fun.
In reality, the moment we step into a space, we are absorbed by it, invisibly adopting its mood and yielding to the irresistible influence of its atmosphere.

I believe that when you introduce playful objects into an environment, it expands the boundaries of the mind. It gives you non-verbal permission to think freely - not just to push against conventional frames, but to forget they even exist.
Below, you will find a selection of artists whose objects are guaranteed to bring an unexpected smile to your face.
Lola Mayeras

French designer Lola Mayeras grew up in the South of France with a ceramist father, so her artistic heritage and exploration of colors and shapes began to form in early childhood. She worked as a fashion designer before launching her own design studio in 2020. During the lockdown, she rediscovered her father’s workshop in her hometown and followed an inner desire to create in a medium familiar to her since youth.

Her background in fashion preserved her love for draping, but now her target objects are furniture and sculptures. Her most frequent signature element is the button-down shirt - it stands still in the form of a vase, is modestly stacked in a sculpture, or effortlessly draped over the corner of a wooden table. The latter is my personal favorite among all her amazing pieces: a restrained, natural ceramic mass with a wrinkled, azure-blue shirt seemingly falling onto the floor.

Lola Mayeras also manages to create anthropomorphic vases with ears and earrings that look perfectly natural an all senses. The balance of form and scale is so fine that it makes you question why other vases lack these symmetrical details. It is bold yet in harmony.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrp9t34bnz37vq.webp

Recently, she has expanded her practice to work with metal and textiles. If you are in search of unique bedding, you can order the “It’s a Mess” set, featuring a trompe-l'œil print of scattered clothes. The light-hearted essence of her objects, along with chosen color palette, is deeply inspired by her childhood in the South of France, where enjoying a sun-filled life was a daily routine.
The light-hearted essence of her objects, along with chosen color palette, is deeply inspired by her childhood in the South of France, where enjoying a sun-filled life was a daily routine.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrp9xqom3fudfj.webp
Erwin Wurm

Erwin Wurm’s work is a prime example of playful irony masking serious social themes – messages that are difficult to read at first glance, but become an inseparable part of the experience once uncovered.

As a pioneer of conceptual humor who has won the hearts of art lovers worldwide, Wurm famously gifts bags, sausages, sweaters, and other everyday items with arms and legs. He is the creator of puffed cars, bloated houses, and anthropomorphic pickles, all reconsidered through simple shapes and actions. This simplicity should by no means diminish the artist's value; rather, it reflects a genuine mastery of a highly readable visual language, which then collides with absolute unpredictability.

Ultimately, the absurdity in Wurm’s art serves as a sharp response to the pressures of contemporary society, such as overconsumption, the overwhelming weight of public opinion, and our obsession with self-representation through the things we own. Underneath the cheerful packaging lies a profound commentary on the modern human condition. Yet, the presence of this hidden depth never compromises the pure, joyful look of his pieces – they remain effortlessly delightful objects that you want to return to again and again.
Yet, the presence of this hidden depth never compromises the pure, joyful look of his pieces – they remain effortlessly delightful objects that you want to return to again and again.
Funny Ollas

Swedish designer Fanny Ollas has a background in textile and fashion, that reflects in her elegantly ornamented vases. Each vessel looks like a fairy character, who live by your side rent-free and has all the rights to do so.

The gentle tones and integration of faux fur, lacing, strass and pearls shape the magical tinkling appearance to every piece, yet they carry a certain state of melancholy. Her work revolves around thoughts about vulnerability, body, demands, fears, relationships and what is hidden behind our facades.
Pablo Picasso

The legendary Spanish artist always called himself an experimenter, and there can't be a more accurate description for the vast broadness of his work. Although he didn’t focus on irony as a core theme, the vessels he produced in large quantities in the South of France at the Madoura Atelier are a perfect reflection of the playful component in the artist's oeuvre.

By the end of World War II, Picasso was already a living legend, an acclaimed genius, and a millionaire. But this success had a backfire effect - he grew tired of academicism and the solemn, rigid attitude toward art. In turning to clay, he seemed to permit himself to become a child again.
"I can draw like Raphael, but it took me a lifetime to learn to draw like a child," - Pablo Picasso

The comical faces he painted on pitchers were an act of pure play and an expression of the absolute happiness he felt while living on the sunny coast with his young muse, Françoise Gilot. After the horrors of war, the tragedy of Guernica, and deep personal crises, creating vibrant, humorous tableware became a form of art therapy for him.

The comical faces he painted on pitchers were an act of pure play and an expression of the absolute happiness he felt while living on the sunny coast with his young muse, Françoise Gilot. After the horrors of war, the tragedy of Guernica, and deep personal crises, creating vibrant, humorous tableware became a form of art therapy for him.

These pitchers were never meant to sit behind glass in dusty museums. Picasso originally intended for his ceramics to be affordable and used in everyday life - for pouring wine or holding fruit - so that people could smile at those amusing, hand-painted faces over breakfast.
Matthew Centeno

Improvisation and an open-minded approach sit at the heart of Matthew Centeno’s creative process. Through highly detailed craftsmanship, he transforms ordinary balloons into captivating shapes that instantly speak directly to the inner child in everyone. His ultimate goal is to break through the monotony of daily life, nudging the audience to rediscover their forgotten sense of curiosity.

While foil balloons are the ultimate indicators of celebrations and holidays, they are inherently temporary. Unlike flowers, which have already become a staple of casual home decor, balloons still belong firmly to the category of special occasions. Centeno's wall-mounted porcelain balloon with a smiling face serves as a permanent reminder that every single day is special.
Sébastien Gaudette

What can be more pleasent than the sticky notes with cheerful inscriptions, that make you feel warm every time you see them? Sebastien Gaudette creates the tromp-l’œil sculptures from aluminium, which will stay on your wall forever. It’s the kind of art that doesn’t have to suit your interior but rather contribute to your mood and emotional well-being. I need to admit that the small size of the work adds to the spark of discovering it around - it’s like a piece of magic which you unexpectedly run into and freeze for a moment to smile for a second and go back to the errands.

The central pillar of the Gaudets' work is not the inscriptions but the recreation of paper folding. However, even within this framework, we find the component of delightful familiarity combined with childish excitement. For example the paper planes of different colors, made from a lined notebook sheet. Finding it on the chest of drawers or coffetable among books and vases would be a wonderful time machine to the carefreeness of youth.
It seems like we are frightened to let the art entartain us.

Whether you are an art - collector, - lover, - enthusiast or just start your acquaintance with bounderless art world, start noticing the objects that not only challange you, question or provocate, but also can evoke warmful memories, create a new one or simply makes you smile almost unreasonably.
Sometimes your joy is an artist goal - surrender to its power.

articles.title: Five Rooms, One Signature
articles.author: EPRIS Journal
articles.excerpt: A dalmatian dot, a slab of burl, three portraits of the same painted dog, and one small cone that keeps reappearing where you least expect it – the disciplined vocabulary one apartment uses five different ways without ever repeating itself.

content.content: Walk through this apartment once and you'll clock the polka dot, the burl veneer, the pair of painted dogs watching from three different walls. Walk through it twice and you'll notice none of them ever appears the same way twice – the dot changes scale on every surface it lands on, the veneer goes from tabletop to cabinet front to a single framed square the size of a postcard, and the dogs shift from grey to black-and-white to a single cropped blue portrait, as if the same idea keeps being translated rather than repeated. That's the real subject here: not a look, but a small, disciplined set of decisions a home can apparently sustain across five very different rooms without ever repeating itself outright.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mrgg0dfmpqmyrg.jpg
content.caption: The dot at its largest scale: a full sectional, upholstered edge to edge, the pattern reading almost as texture before it reads as pattern.

content.content: Up close, this is not a printed polka dot – it's drawn, each mark an irregular blot with its own weight and edge, the kind of variation that happens when a hand repeats a gesture rather than a machine repeating a die-cut.
